opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think probabilistic computation is everywhere in AI today, but we mostly don't acknowledge it as such. If you look at what a large language model actually does at inference time, the final step is sampling: you get a distribution over tokens and you draw from it. Diffusion models are literally learning to reverse a noising process, a stochastic dynamical system. Even training is fundamentally noisy; stochastic gradient descent works partly *because* of the noise, which helps you explore the loss landscape and find flatter, more generalizable minima.

So the workloads are deeply probabilistic. The problem is the hardware isn't. We've spent decades and enormous engineering effort building digital machines that suppress noise at every level. We push transistors far above the thermal noise floor so every bit is deterministic, and then we spend huge amounts of compute and energy using pseudo-random number generators and matrix multiplications to *simulate* randomness and probability distributions. That's a strange inversion. Nature hands us stochasticity for free at small scales, and we pay a big energy tax to eliminate it, only to rebuild it in software.

The way I see it, the frontier is going to involve hardware that embraces the physics rather than fighting it: systems where the natural thermal fluctuations of the device become the source of sampling, where the dynamics of the hardware itself relax toward a distribution you care about. Energy-based models are a natural fit, because you can map the energy function onto the physical system and let thermodynamics do the sampling for you.

Why does this matter? Energy efficiency, mainly. If you believe, as I do, that intelligence scales with our ability to harness energy and turn it into useful computation, then how many joules per useful sample becomes one of the most important numbers in civilization. Today's AI is bottlenecked by power and by the cost of moving bits around deterministically. Probabilistic, physics-based computing could get you orders of magnitude better efficiency for the generative parts of the workload.

I don't think it replaces GPUs wholesale. Deterministic digital compute is great for many things. But I think we'll move toward a heterogeneous stack, where the parts of AI that are fundamentally about sampling, uncertainty, and generative modeling run on substrates that are native to probability. That's the bet: stop simulating randomness and start computing with it.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that almost everything we do in modern AI is, at its core, probabilistic. We're sampling from distributions. Language models are sampling tokens from a learned distribution. Diffusion models are literally running a stochastic process in reverse to denoise. Bayesian inference, Monte Carlo methods, reinforcement learning with exploration, all of these are fundamentally about generating and manipulating randomness.

And yet we're running all of that on hardware that was designed to be as deterministic as possible. We spend an enormous amount of energy in CPUs and GPUs suppressing noise. We build transistors and cooling systems and error correction all to make sure a bit is exactly a zero or exactly a one. Then, in software, we go and spend even more compute generating pseudo-random numbers to put the noise back in. That's the irony. We're paying twice: once to kill the entropy, and again to synthesize it.

So the question we've been asking is, what if you embraced the physics? Nature at the mesoscale is noisy for free. Thermal fluctuations are everywhere. If you can build circuits where the stochasticity is a feature rather than a bug, where the physical state of the device is itself a sample from the distribution you care about, then sampling becomes something the hardware just does, rather than something you simulate at great cost. That's the idea behind thermodynamic computing, and I think of it as a kind of middle path between classical digital and quantum. Quantum computing tries to harness coherence and superposition, which is extraordinarily hard to protect. Thermodynamic computing harnesses noise, which is extraordinarily easy to get.

Where this becomes relevant for today's workloads is that a lot of the bottleneck in things like diffusion sampling, Bayesian deep learning, or even just linear algebra primitives that can be reformulated as equilibrium or sampling problems, is exactly the kind of thing a physical stochastic system can do natively. You let the system relax to equilibrium and read out the answer. The energy cost scales very differently from pushing bits through a von Neumann architecture.

Now, I'll be the first to say this isn't going to replace GPUs for every matrix multiply tomorrow. Deterministic digital compute is phenomenal at what it does. But I think the next big leap in efficiency isn't going to come from shrinking transistors further. It's going to come from matching the hardware to the mathematical structure of the problem. And if the structure of the problem is probabilistic, which in AI it overwhelmingly is, then building probabilistic hardware is the natural move. We've spent decades fighting entropy. I think the next era is about putting it to work.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to distinguish between reasoning about probabilities and actually computing probabilistically. A lot of today’s AI is probabilistic in the first sense: we train models to represent distributions, and we sample from those distributions to generate outputs. But underneath, much of the work is still deterministic linear algebra running on GPUs.

That raises an interesting question: where should randomness enter the computation? Is it something you add at the end when you sample a token, or could it be a resource throughout the computational process?

For workloads where sampling is central, you can imagine hardware that uses physical fluctuations to explore a distribution. The challenge is making those fluctuations useful and controllable. You need the system to sample from the distribution you actually want, and you need to account for the cost of getting information into and out of it.

So I see probabilistic computation as a potential complement to the current stack. The interesting question is which parts of an AI workload are naturally sampling problems, and whether we can execute those parts more efficiently by treating randomness as a computational resource.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to distinguish between computing probabilities and actually computing probabilistically. Most of our AI hardware is deterministic: we do these enormous matrix multiplications to train a model that represents a probability distribution. Then, at the output, we sample from that distribution.

But you can ask: could randomness become a resource throughout the computation? Could the physical dynamics of a system help us generate samples, rather than having to simulate that process with a lot of deterministic operations?

That’s particularly interesting for workloads where you care about uncertainty, or where there are many plausible answers and you want to explore them. The challenge is that producing randomness is easy; producing samples from the particular distribution you want, efficiently and controllably, is hard. So the opportunity is to co-design the model, the algorithm, and the hardware around that task.
